The Simpsons. An animated sitcom that premiered on Fox in nineteen eighty-nine following the dysfunctional Simpson family—Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and baby Maggie—in the fictional town of Springfield. Using animation to bypass the constraints of live-action sitcoms, the show perfected satirical comedy rooted in family dysfunction, consumer culture, and American mediocrity, while maintaining genuine emotional stakes between family members.

Created by Matt Groening, who developed the characters from his comic strip Life in Hell and originally debuted them as a segment on The Tracey Ullman Show in nineteen eighty-seven. Dan Castellaneta voiced Homer Simpson, the bumbling father whose stupidity and love for his family drove the show's emotional center. Animation allowed visual gags and satirical exaggeration impossible in live-action comedies. The show's humor was multilayered: jokes for children, cultural references for adults, and sophisticated satirical commentary on American consumer culture.

Each episode is set on the same day of the week—Sunday—in a fictional perpetual present, allowing the show to age without the characters aging. The Simpsons won thirty-nine Emmy Awards and countless accolades; its cultural references and quotes permeate American discourse. The show achieved global cultural dominance; it airs in nearly two hundred countries and is considered the most-watched television program in history.
